c.tagline: A romantic canal town of glass, music boxes, and fresh Hokkaido seafood

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are reliable and metered but expensive by Western standards; most useful late at night or when carrying luggage in winter.

emergency.note: Japan's emergency services are fast and reliable; English support is improving but not guaranteed outside major hospitals.

hood_desc: The city's postcard image: a restored 1920s canal lined with old stone warehouses, gas lamps, and willow trees, especially atmospheric when lit up at night. It's the most-photographed spot in Otaru and the heart of the tourist district.

A preserved Meiji- and Taisho-era merchant street lined with former banks and trading houses, now selling music boxes, hand-blown glass, and Otaru's famous sushi and soft-serve ice cream. It's the main shopping strip for souvenirs and crafts.

The transit hub of the city, anchored by JR Otaru Station's landmark 1934 building with its gas-lamp motif interior. Shops, izakayas, and easy access to Sapporo trains make it a practical, central base.

A quieter residential area built around the former Temiya rail line, Hokkaido's first railway, now preserved as a walking and cycling path. It offers a low-key, local slice of Otaru away from the canal crowds.

A former herring-fishing district on Otaru's coast, home to the Otaru Aquarium and the preserved Nishin Goten herring mansion. Its rocky coastline and small beaches make it a relaxed spot for sea views.

water.note: Tap water is safe and good quality, as everywhere in Japan.

transit.note: Otaru Station connects to Sapporo in about 30-40 minutes by train; the historic canal area itself is compact and walkable.

train: JR Hakodate Main Line links Otaru directly to Sapporo and New Chitose Airport
bus: Chuo Bus connects Otaru to Sapporo and the airport
ferry: New Otaru Ferry Terminal serves long-distance ferries to Maizuru and Niigata

tip.r: Tipping is not practiced in Japan and can even be considered rude or confusing; excellent service is simply the norm.
